column6: The commentary labels ar-Raḥmān and ar-Raḥīm with Arabic root r-ḥ-m; YHWH names himself raḥum and gracious here, giving the mercy cognate a divine self-description.
The commentary's mercy words share a Semitic root with Moses' raḥum; Deuteronomy grounds that compassion in God's refusal to abandon the covenant people.
The commentary repeats mercy in 1:1 and 1:3; Lamentations uses the cognate raḥamim for compassion that has not ended, renewed each morning.
The commentary makes mercy the source of bestowed good; the psalm describes YHWH as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.

The commentary labels anʿamta with Arabic n-ʿ-m and glosses the gift as a good state; the cognate Hebrew pleasantness word describes the allotted inheritance as pleasant places, though it does not mean a bestowed favor here.
The commentary calls the bestowed favor a path-gift; the cognate Hebrew noʿam describes Wisdom's ways as pleasant and her paths as peace, a limited lexical bridge to the commentary's path image.

The commentary identifies Rabb as the giver who completes beneficence; Daniel's Aramaic cognate rav means chief or superior for Daniel's appointment, showing related lordly rank language without the commentary's beneficence sense.
The commentary pictures niʿma as a hand extending good; Israel's creed says God brought them out with a strong hand and outstretched arm, naming the rescue behind their received good.
The commentary says the gift becomes a community's path; Israel recounts being brought into a land flowing with milk and honey before presenting its first fruits.
The commentary says the recipient answers a gift with hamd; the offerer sets the first fruits before God and bows, turning received land into a grateful act.
The commentary makes a bestowed favor belong to a community; Israel rejoices in every good received with Levite and resident alien, extending the response to fellow recipients.
The commentary says praise answers received favor; Moses commands Israel to eat, be satisfied, and bless YHWH for the good land.
The commentary contrasts praise of the giver with forgetting the gift; Moses warns that fullness can lead Israel to forget YHWH.
The commentary warns against claiming one's own spending as a favor; Moses anticipates Israel saying its own power made its wealth.
The commentary locates the gift in its giver; Moses tells Israel to remember YHWH, who gives the power to make wealth and confirms the covenant.
The commentary's hamd includes telling another person the giver's good acts; Moses recounts to Jethro what YHWH did for Israel and the hardships from which he rescued them.
The commentary pictures praise of the benefactor in another's presence; Jethro rejoices at the good YHWH has done for Israel after hearing Moses' account.
The commentary links reporting God's favor with praise; Jethro blesses YHWH before naming the rescue from Egypt and Pharaoh.

column5: praise and thanks for received gifts
column6: The commentary places hamd before the named favor; David's assembly blesses God's glorious name and gives thanks for all that comes from him.
The commentary treats the recipient's praise as an answer to favor; David says that all things come from God and that the offering is given from what is already God's.

column5: giving from what belongs to God
column6: The commentary depicts the giver's good passing to a recipient; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says to give God what is God's, since the person and possessions are God's, interpreting David's words in 1 Chronicles 29:14.

column5: blessing before benefiting from the world
column6: The commentary says hamd answers a received favor; the rabbis rule that one may not enjoy worldly benefit without a blessing, making praise a recognition of God's ownership and gift.
The commentary says the recipient recounts the benefactor's goodness before others; the rescued speaker promises to tell God's name to his brothers and praise him in the congregation.

column5: poor eat, are satisfied, and praise
column6: The commentary joins received provision to praise; in the same psalm's assembly the poor eat and are satisfied, and those seeking God praise him.
The commentary distinguishes recounting God's favors from boasting in one's own giving; the psalmist's soul boasts in YHWH, so the humble hear and rejoice.
The commentary makes praise the recipient's response; the psalmist magnifies YHWH and reports that God answered and delivered him from fear.
The commentary's hamd includes telling others about the giver's favors; the psalmist invites God-fearers to hear what God did for him.

column5: making God's deeds known among peoples
column6: The commentary says the benefactor's kindnesses are recounted to others; the psalm commands thanks to YHWH and making his deeds known among the peoples.
The commentary's praise names the giver's good before others; the psalm calls for singing and telling all God's wondrous works.
The commentary says praise answers received good; worshippers enter with thanksgiving and praise, naming God as their benefactor.
The commentary roots good in mercy; the psalm grounds praise in God's goodness and enduring steadfast love.
The commentary says recipients recount the giver's favors; the psalmist tells his own soul not to forget all God's benefits.
The commentary describes nimah as good bestowed on a recipient; the psalm names forgiveness and healing among God's benefits.
The commentary pictures favor as a gift reaching its recipient; the psalm says God redeems life and crowns the speaker with steadfast love and compassion.
The commentary's secondary gloss says giving can mean adding beyond enough; the psalm says God satisfies life with good and renews youth.
The commentary labels its repeated ar-Raḥmān/ar-Raḥīm with Arabic r-ḥ-m; this psalm uses the cognate compassion language alongside grace and abundant steadfast love.

column5: thanks for steadfast love and wonders
column6: The commentary says beneficiaries recount good received; the psalm repeatedly calls the redeemed to thank YHWH for his steadfast love and wonderful works.
The commentary says the giver's favor reaches a needy recipient; the psalm says God satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good.
The commentary makes hamd the recipient's answer to favor; the psalmist asks what he can return to YHWH for all his benefits.
The commentary includes telling God's favors before others; the psalmist fulfills his vows to YHWH in the presence of all God's people.
The commentary makes divine mercy the source of good; the psalm praises YHWH as gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and great in steadfast love.
The commentary visualizes a hand extending a gift; the psalm says God opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing.
The commentary says the recipient's praise names the benefactor; the psalm ends by calling all flesh to bless God's holy name forever.

column5: asking to be shown God's ways
column6: The commentary calls the bestowed favor a path-gift; the psalmist asks God to make his ways known.
The commentary says the gift is completed by walking the path; the psalm asks God to lead and teach the speaker because God is his salvation.

column5: all paths are love and faithfulness
column6: The commentary joins divine favor to the path; the psalm says all YHWH's paths are steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant.
The commentary names Rabb as the one completing good and making the recipient's way possible; the psalm calls YHWH shepherd and says the speaker lacks nothing.
The commentary calls the bestowed favor a path-gift; the shepherd psalm says God restores the soul and leads the speaker in right paths.
The commentary asks for the path of those favored and distinguishes them from the other groups; the psalm contrasts the way YHWH knows with the way of the wicked that perishes.
The commentary calls the gift a path on which one walks; Proverbs depicts the righteous person's way as a light growing brighter toward day.
The commentary sets the favored path against those who stray; Proverbs contrasts the dark way of the wicked, who stumble without knowing what made them fall.
The commentary asks for the path of the favored rather than the opposing path; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life.

column5: loving and holding fast to God
column6: The commentary says the gift is completed by walking the path; Moses identifies life with loving, obeying, and holding fast to YHWH.

column5: hearts that stray and do not know God's ways
column6: The commentary distinguishes those who receive guidance from those who stray; the psalm identifies the wilderness generation by their wandering hearts and failure to know God's ways.

column5: divine anger and exclusion from rest
column6: The commentary names those under anger as the contrary group; the psalm's wilderness oracle ends with God's oath that they will not enter his rest.

column5: we strayed from the way of truth
column6: The commentary contrasts the sought path with those who stray; the wicked in Wisdom confess that they left the way of truth and righteousness.
The commentary excludes those who lose the way; the same confession says the wicked wearied themselves on paths of lawlessness, giving the wandering a moral setting.

column5: the broad way leading to destruction
column6: The commentary asks for one path and distinguishes its recipients from those astray; Jesus says the wide gate and broad way lead to destruction.

column5: the narrow way leading to life
column6: The commentary asks for the path of the favored; Jesus contrasts the narrow gate and hard way that lead to life.
The commentary makes hamd the answer to received favor; Zechariah begins by blessing Israel's God for visiting and redeeming his people.
The commentary connects the path of the favored to divine mercy; Zechariah says the redemption enacts mercy promised to the ancestors and remembrance of the covenant.
The commentary says mercy is the source of beneficence; Zechariah attributes the coming dawn to the tender mercy of God.

column5: guiding feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary joins received favor to a path; Zechariah says the dawn will guide feet into the way of peace.
The commentary says the path is a favor received from God; Paul describes salvation as grace through faith and God's gift.

column5: no boasting in one's own works
column6: The commentary rejects claiming one's own expenditure as a favor; Paul excludes boasting because salvation is not from works.
The commentary says the favor is completed by walking the path; Paul says God made believers for good works prepared for them to walk in.
The commentary's B002 gloss on Rabb is completion of beneficence and its path ends in walking; Paul trusts God to complete the good work begun in the believers until Christ's day.
The commentary says praise answers a gift and its B010 gloss includes giving more; Jesus gives thanks, distributes the loaves, and feeds the crowd.
The commentary says anʿama can mean adding beyond enough; after the crowd is filled, Jesus orders the surplus fragments gathered so none is lost.

column5: fullness received as grace upon grace
column6: The commentary's secondary gloss says a gift may be increased beyond measure; John says all received from Christ's fullness, grace upon grace.

column5: thanks for grace given in Christ
column6: The commentary makes praise the response to a received gift; Paul thanks God for grace given to the Corinthian believers in Christ.

column5: God sustains believers to the end
column6: The commentary links a completed favor to a walked path; Paul says Christ will strengthen the community to the end, blameless at his day.

column5: what was received leaves no ground to boast
column6: The commentary warns against advertising what one spent as one's own merit; Paul asks what anyone has that was not received and rejects boasting as though it were not received.

column5: failure to glorify or give thanks
column6: The commentary presents praise as the due answer to received good; Paul describes people who knew God yet neither glorified him nor gave thanks.
The commentary says mercy is the source of the favor that guides a person; Paul says God's kindness, forbearance, and patience lead toward repentance.
The commentary warns against self-praise for a favor received; Paul tells grafted-in Gentiles not to boast over the natural branches because the root supports them.

The commentary distinguishes those receiving favor from those under anger; Paul sets God's kindness toward believers beside severity toward those who fell, and warns the former to continue in kindness.

column5: the healed man glorifies God aloud
column6: The commentary says the recipient recounts the giver's favor; one healed leper returns, loudly glorifying God.
The commentary makes hamd the recipient's answer to a gift; the Samaritan falls at Jesus' feet and thanks him after healing.

column5: the foreigner returns to praise God
column6: The commentary says praise of the benefactor should be voiced; Jesus asks whether only the foreigner returned to give glory to God.

column5: food, gladness, and witness to God's goodness
column6: The commentary connects divine favor to the provision of good; Paul says God gave rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness, leaving witness among the nations.

column5: grace multiplying thanksgiving to God's glory
column6: The commentary says the recipient's praise follows God's favor; Paul says grace reaching more people multiplies thanksgiving to God's glory.
The commentary's B010 branch says giving may exceed what is sufficient; Paul says God can make grace abound so believers have sufficiency for every good work.
The commentary says the giver's good reaches a recipient who praises; Paul says generosity enriches the giver and produces thanksgiving to God through the recipients.
The commentary links conveyed good with praise of its source; Paul says the service supplies the saints' needs and overflows in many thanksgivings to God.
The commentary depicts beneficiaries recounting the giver's good; Paul says recipients glorify God for the donors' confession and generous sharing.
The commentary says praise answers a gift; Paul closes the account of giving by thanking God for his inexpressible gift.

column5: called from darkness to proclaim praises
column6: The commentary asks for the path of people favored by God; Peter describes a people called from darkness into marvelous light to proclaim God's excellencies.

column5: once not a people, now recipients of mercy
column6: The commentary identifies a community by the favor it received; Peter says those once outside the people have become God's people and have received mercy.

column5: blessing God for new birth and hope
column6: The commentary makes hamd the answer to a favor; Peter blesses God for new birth to a living hope through Jesus' resurrection.
The commentary says the favor belongs to a community and its path; Peter names an imperishable inheritance kept in heaven for believers.

column5: faith tested toward praise and honor
column6: The commentary makes the path end in a completed favor; Peter says tested faith will result in praise, glory, and honor at Jesus' revelation.

column5: thanksgiving and praise before the throne
column6: The commentary places hamd as the fitting answer to God's favor; the heavenly assembly ascribes blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might to God.

column5: the Lamb shepherds and guides to water
column6: The commentary joins divine favor with a path; the Lamb shepherds the multitude and guides them to springs of living water.
The commentary distinguishes recounting God's favors from holding one's own generosity over people; Jesus warns that public almsgiving for recognition receives its reward from people.

column5: the giver does not advertise the gift
column6: The commentary condemns self-credit for one's spending; Jesus says the giver's left hand should not know what the right hand gives.
The commentary contrasts service with self-praise; Jesus says secret giving is seen and rewarded by the Father.
The commentary distinguishes praise of the giver from claiming one's own merit; the Pharisee thanks God while boasting that he is unlike other people.

column5: the self-exalting and humble are reversed
column6: The commentary contrasts benefactor-praise with self-praise; Jesus says the self-exalting Pharisee is not justified, while the humble tax collector is.

column5: do not add reproach to a gift
column6: The commentary describes hamd's reverse as rubbing one's favor in another's face; Ben Sira directly says not to add reproach or hurtful words when doing good or giving.
The commentary warns that the recipient can be humiliated by a favor held over them; Ben Sira says a gift from a grudging person dims the eyes, showing how manner changes the gift.
The commentary pictures good passing from one hand to another; the king has compassion and cancels a servant's debt, a received favor that sets up the servant's obligation toward another.

column5: failure to pass received mercy onward
column6: The commentary says an act of kindness is carried to another; the king condemns the forgiven servant for failing to show his fellow servant the mercy he received.
The commentary says mercy is the source of beneficence; Jesus describes God as kind even to the ungrateful and evil, then commands love of enemies.
The commentary presents receiving God's mercy as the ground of a favored way; Jesus tells disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful.

column5: love as a response to prior love
column6: The commentary makes the recipient's response follow the giver's favor; John says believers love because God first loved them.

column5: received goods shared with a brother
column6: The commentary's hand-to-hand image traces good from giver to recipient; John asks how God's love can remain in someone who sees a needy brother and closes the heart despite possessing the world's goods.

column5: love enacted rather than merely spoken
column6: The commentary contrasts genuine praise and giving with words that claim merit; John requires love in deed and truth, giving the response a practical form.

column5: bless God for all his works
column6: The commentary makes praise the recipient's answer to God's favor; Ben Sira blesses the God who does great things everywhere and asks that God grant joy of heart.

column5: declare God's greatness among the nations
column6: The commentary says God's favor should be told to others; Tobit calls Israel to declare God's greatness before the nations and praise him in Jerusalem.
The commentary joins received mercy with a public response; Tobit says those who turn to God with their whole heart will bless him in truth.
The commentary makes hamd the recipient's response to a gift; the community's meal prayer gives thanks over the cup and broken bread as gifts from God through Jesus.

column5: gathering the Church as one people
column6: The commentary says favor belongs to a community and its path; the Eucharistic prayer asks that the scattered Church be gathered into God's kingdom, like bread once scattered and made one.

column5: thanksgiving for gifts of knowledge and life
column6: The commentary says praise follows what God gives; after the meal the community thanks the holy Father for his name, knowledge, faith, and immortality given through Jesus.

column5: the prayer ends in glory to God
column6: The commentary says the opening hamd returns at the end of the path; the Didache's thanksgiving closes by ascribing glory to God forever.

column5: praise as the creature's response to its maker
column6: The commentary places hamd before naming the specific gift; Augustine opens by praising God as creator and says human beings are made for God, so praise is the fitting response to dependence itself.
The commentary says recipients answer good with praise; after Israel is rescued from Egypt, Moses and Israel sing to YHWH about the victory.
The commentary's praise names the giver and his good; the song calls YHWH strength, song, and salvation, joining worship to received deliverance.

column5: anger turns and comfort is received
column6: The commentary distinguishes those under anger from those given favor; Isaiah's rescued speaker says God's anger has turned away and he has comforted him.
The commentary says one should recount the giver's favor; Isaiah calls the people to thank YHWH and make his deeds known among the peoples.
The commentary's hamd is voiced before others; Isaiah calls the people to sing because God has done gloriously and make it known throughout the earth.

column5: rejoicing in the Holy One among the people
column6: The commentary links divine favor to a community's road; Isaiah calls Zion to shout and sing because the Holy One is great in Israel's midst.
The commentary says the recipient's answer is praise; Isaiah says the people God formed are to recount God's praise.

column5: God teaches the way to walk
column6: The commentary says the favor is a path-gift; Isaiah names YHWH as teacher who leads Israel in the way it should go.

column5: being led out in joy and peace
column6: The commentary says the gift is completed by walking the way; Isaiah depicts the redeemed going out with joy and being led in peace.
The commentary says praise can tell others the giver's favors; Isaiah's speaker publicly recounts YHWH's acts of steadfast love and praise for Israel.
The commentary makes mercy the source of good bestowed on a people; Isaiah says God saved them in love and pity and carried them through their days.

column5: boasting in strength or wealth is rejected
column6: The commentary rejects making one's own expenditure a public merit; Jeremiah says the wise, mighty, and rich must not boast in their own wisdom, power, or riches.

column5: boast only in knowing the God who does kindness
column6: The commentary says praise should name the benefactor's goodness; Jeremiah permits boasting only in understanding and knowing YHWH, who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness.
The commentary says hamd reaches beyond thanking for a particular material gift; Habakkuk imagines the loss of figs, grapes, olives, fields, and flock.
The commentary's praise is directed to the giver rather than only to goods; Habakkuk rejoices in YHWH and exults in the God of salvation despite the failed harvest.

column5: Pharaoh's daughter, rather than Pharaoh, adopts Moses
column6: The commentary recalls Pharaoh claiming Moses' upbringing as a favor; Exodus says Pharaoh's daughter draws the child from the water and adopts him, shifting the rescuer from the king to his daughter.
The commentary's Pharaoh reproaches Moses with a personal favor while Moses answers with Israel's oppression; Exodus presents Pharaoh as the ruler who sets taskmasters over Israel.
The commentary says Moses answers the favor-reproach by naming Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; Exodus narrates the Egyptians' ruthless forced labor as the background that reverses the king's claim.

column5: Pharaoh's daughter takes Moses as her son
column6: The commentary places the claim of raising Moses in Pharaoh's mouth; Stephen's retelling attributes his rescue and adoption to Pharaoh's daughter, preserving the household upbringing but changing the agent.

column5: Moses refuses the status of Pharaoh's daughter's son
column6: The commentary presents a royal upbringing invoked as a favor; Hebrews says Moses later refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, emphasizing his break with that household identity.

column5: compassion shown beyond the expected group
column6: The commentary asks for the path of those favored; Jonah resents God's graciousness and compassion toward Nineveh, exposing the tension over who receives mercy.

column5: Jeshurun grows full and forgets the giver
column6: The commentary warns that good must be answered with praise rather than taken for granted; Moses says Jeshurun grew fat, then forsook the God who made him.

column5: he people receive provision from heaven
column6: The commentary describes favor as good conveyed to a recipient; the psalm says God opened heaven and rained manna to feed Israel.

column5: the people remain ungrateful after wonders
column6: The commentary makes praise the fitting response to received benefits; despite God's wonders, the people continue to sin and fail to trust.
The commentary distinguishes divine mercy from anger; the psalm says God is compassionate, forgives, and often turns away his anger from the people.

column5: merciful and gracious remembrance of wonders
column6: The commentary links mercy with the praise-worthy giver; the psalm says God made his wonders remembered and is gracious and compassionate.

column5: thanks for God's goodness and enduring love
column6: The commentary says praise answers received good; the litany begins by thanking God for goodness and repeats enduring love through its account of creation and deliverance.
The commentary's ar-Raḥmān/ar-Raḥīm share the Semitic mercy root with the psalm's raḥum; the verse describes God's compassion, patience, and great love.

column5: Moses' mercy attributes become a repeated prayer form
column6: The commentary repeats the mercy formula in 1:1 and 1:3; the rabbis read Exodus 34:6 as the order of divine attributes Moses was taught to invoke whenever Israel sins and seeks forgiveness.

column5: bowing and worship after the mercy formula
column6: The commentary presents mercy as the source of good and hamd as the response; after YHWH proclaims compassion, Moses bows to the ground and worships.

column5: mercy requested for a people on the way
column6: The commentary links the favor of a people to their path; Moses asks God to go among them, pardon their sin, and take them as his inheritance.
The commentary makes praise the recipient's answer to favor; after Samuel's birth Hannah rejoices in YHWH and his salvation, telling of God's reversal of her condition.
The commentary describes hamd as response to a gift; David asks who he is and what his house is that God has brought him this far, receiving the promised future as undeserved good.
The commentary says praise names the benefactor; David declares that there is no one like YHWH and no God besides him after hearing the promise to his house.
The commentary says the recipient recognizes the giver's good; David calls God's words true and recalls that God has promised this good to his servant.

column5: land received without the people's labor
column6: The commentary describes favor as good conveyed to a community; Joshua recalls that God gave Israel land, cities, vineyards, and olive groves they had not made or planted.
The commentary makes worship an answer to benefit; Joshua therefore tells Israel to fear and serve YHWH sincerely, remembering God's prior acts.
The commentary asks for the way of those favored; Joshua puts rival forms of service before Israel and calls the people to choose whom they will serve.

column5: remembering great deeds as a reason to serve
column6: The commentary makes praise the recipient's answer to good; Samuel tells Israel to fear and serve YHWH faithfully and consider the great things he has done for them.

The commentary says the recipient's praise returns at the journey's end; after God turns mourning into dancing, the psalmist says his soul will sing praise and give thanks forever. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)
The commentary says God's favors are recounted before others; the psalmist does not hide God's deliverance, faithfulness, and love from the great congregation. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

column5: blessing that makes God's way known
column6: The commentary joins a bestowed favor to a path; the psalm asks God to bless the people so that God's way and saving power become known on earth. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

column5: nations rejoice under God's just guidance
column6: The commentary asks for a path of divine favor; the psalm calls the nations to rejoice because God judges peoples with equity and guides the nations on earth. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

column5: blessing that reaches the ends of the earth
column6: The commentary describes a community receiving favor; the psalm asks God to bless Israel so that all the ends of the earth fear him. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

The commentary's account of hamd includes telling another person the giver's goodness; this verse says the speaker has not concealed God's steadfast love and faithfulness from the assembly. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)
The commentary calls the received favor a path-gift; pilgrims crossing the Valley of Baca make it a spring, and the early rain covers it with blessings. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

column5: God's love and faithfulness told for generations
column6: The commentary says the benefactor's good is told aloud; the psalmist says he will sing of YHWH's steadfast love and make his faithfulness known through every generation. (Hebrew WLC numbering.)

column5: compassion pictured as a father's care
column6: The commentary grounds good in mercy; the psalm compares YHWH's compassion for those who fear him to a father's compassion for his children.
The commentary includes recounting a giver's favor before others; the psalm tells the redeemed to offer thanksgiving sacrifices and tell God's works with songs of joy.

column5: thanksgiving as a public act of worship
column6: The commentary makes hamd the response to a received benefit; the psalmist offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name after asking how to repay God's benefits.
The commentary says recipients tell the benefactor's kindnesses; the psalm says they pour out the memory of God's abundant goodness and sing of his righteousness.
The commentary presents mercy as the source of bestowed good; the psalm says YHWH is good to all and his compassion extends to all he has made.

column5: happiness grounded in God as helper
column6: The commentary identifies the favored as a people whose good comes from God; the psalm calls blessed the person whose help is the God of Jacob and whose hope rests in YHWH.
The commentary's image is good reaching a recipient; the psalm praises God who executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry.
The commentary calls favor a path on which one walks; Isaiah says the way of the righteous is level and God makes it smooth.

column5: the Holy Way for the redeemed
column6: The commentary asks for the path of those given favor; Isaiah depicts a holy highway on which the redeemed walk and from which the unclean are excluded.

column5: the redeemed return with praise and joy
column6: The commentary says the path ends in completed favor; Isaiah says YHWH's ransomed return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy.
The commentary links mercy, provision, and a path; Isaiah says the compassionate one guides the redeemed and leads them beside springs of water so they do not hunger or thirst.
The commentary makes mercy the source of favor; YHWH says he has loved Israel with an everlasting love and drawn the people with steadfast love.

column5: leading the people on a straight path
column6: The commentary says the favor is completed by walking a way; YHWH leads the returning people by streams of water on a straight path where they will not stumble.

column5: mercy despite a people's refusal to follow
column6: The commentary distinguishes the favored path from those who stray; Nehemiah's prayer recounts Israel's rebellion yet calls God gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.
The commentary links a bestowed good to guidance along the way; Nehemiah's prayer says God gave his good spirit to instruct the people and supplied manna and water.

column5: fullness and delight in great goodness
column6: The commentary says recipients should answer favor with praise; Nehemiah recalls that Israel ate, was filled, and delighted in God's great goodness.

The commentary contrasts the guided community with those who reject the way; Nehemiah says Israel became disobedient and killed the prophets who warned them after God had given them rest and abundance.
The commentary presents mercy as a source of continuing favor; Nehemiah says God did not make a complete end of Israel or abandon them because of his great mercies.

column5: God delights in mercy and forgives
column6: The commentary connects divine mercy to the favored community; Micah praises the God who pardons iniquity and does not retain anger forever because he delights in steadfast love.
The commentary describes mercy as good reaching its recipients; Micah says God again has compassion and casts the people's sins away.

column5: steadfast love kept to the ancestors
column6: The commentary treats favor as a communal inheritance; Micah says God keeps faith and steadfast love promised to Abraham and Jacob.

column5: Mary magnifies God in response to favor
column6: The commentary says the receiver answers a gift with praise; Mary publicly magnifies the Lord and rejoices in God her savior.

column5: God has done great things for Mary
column6: The commentary's hamd recounts the giver's good; Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her and names his holiness.
The commentary presents mercy as the source of blessing; Mary says God's mercy extends from generation to generation to those who fear him.

column5: God raises the lowly and brings down rulers
column6: The commentary distinguishes those given favor from the contrary way; Mary's song describes God reversing status by bringing rulers down and exalting the lowly.
The commentary says favor is a gift delivered to recipients; Mary sings that God fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty.

column5: sun and rain given to just and unjust
column6: The commentary identifies mercy as the source of good; Jesus says the Father gives sun and rain to both evil and good, extending divine beneficence beyond a single favored group.

column5: freely received good freely passed on
column6: The commentary pictures favor passing from hand to hand; Jesus tells disciples that what they received freely they should give freely as they heal and proclaim.

column5: the healed man walks and praises God
column6: The commentary joins a received favor to its path and response; the healed man enters the temple walking and leaping while praising God.

column5: the public sees the recipient praising
column6: The commentary says the beneficiary can voice praise before others; everyone sees the formerly lame man walking and praising God.

column5: God gives life and breath to all
column6: The commentary describes the giver as the source of good; Paul says God is not served as though needy, since he himself gives all people life, breath, and everything.

column5: no one first gives to God
column6: The commentary says the beneficiary answers a gift with praise rather than claiming merit; Paul asks who has ever given God something first so that God must repay.

column5: all things come from God and return to him
column6: The commentary makes the giver's favor the source and goal of the recipient's path; Paul says all things are from, through, and for God, to whom glory belongs.

column5: work attributed to grace rather than self
column6: The commentary warns against presenting one's own effort as a merit; Paul says he worked hard, yet attributes what he is and his work to God's grace.
The commentary names mercy as the source of good; Paul blesses the Father of mercies and God of all comfort.

column5: comfort received and passed to others
column6: The commentary pictures beneficence moving from giver to recipient; Paul says God comforts believers so they can comfort others in the trouble they themselves have received comfort through.

column5: thanks for a share in the inheritance
column6: The commentary says a community receives a path and a gift; Paul gives thanks to the Father who qualified believers to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.

column5: transfer from darkness into a kingdom
column6: The commentary contrasts the favored path with those astray; Paul says God rescued believers from the authority of darkness and transferred them into the Son's kingdom.
The commentary says favor is completed by walking its path; Paul tells believers to walk in Christ Jesus, whom they received.
The commentary joins the path of favor to praise; Paul describes believers as rooted and built up in Christ, abounding in thanksgiving.
The commentary says a gift can be ruined by holding it over its recipient; James says God gives wisdom generously to all and does not reproach the one who asks.

column5: every good gift comes from above
column6: The commentary says all good reaches the recipient from its giver; James says every good giving and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights.

column5: divine power grants what leads to life
column6: The commentary joins bestowed favor with a path to walk; Peter says God's power has granted everything needed for life and godliness, calling believers by glory and excellence.

column5: riches are gifts, not grounds for pride
column6: The commentary rejects self-credit for what one has received; Paul tells the rich not to be arrogant but to hope in God, who richly provides all things to enjoy.

column5: received wealth used generously for others
column6: The commentary depicts good passing from hand to hand; Paul tells the wealthy to do good, be generous, and ready to share.

column5: stewarding a gift for one another
column6: The commentary pictures favor as good delivered to another; Peter tells each person to use the gift received to serve others as a steward of God's varied grace.

column5: salvation from mercy rather than deeds
column6: The commentary makes divine mercy the source of favor; Titus says God saved people through mercy, not righteous works they had done.

column5: grace makes recipients heirs in hope
column6: The commentary says favor is a gift that carries a community toward its end; Titus says believers justified by grace become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

column5: praise voiced as the fruit of lips
column6: The commentary says the recipient should recount the benefactor's good; Hebrews calls believers to offer continual praise to God, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
The commentary asks for a path that does not stray; Jude praises God who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless.

column5: glory to the only God at the journey's end
column6: The commentary says the opening praise returns at the end of the path; Jude's closing doxology gives glory, majesty, power, and authority to God through Jesus Christ.

column5: creatures acknowledge the giver of all things
column6: The commentary makes praise the response to God's favor; the heavenly elders worship the creator because all things exist by his will.

column5: salvation belongs to God and the Lamb
column6: The commentary names a community by the favor it received; the multitude cries that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb before the elders' full doxology.

column5: blessing God for adversity as well as good
column6: The commentary says hamd is broader than thanks for a discrete favor; the Mishnah requires a blessing for bad events as for good, extending praise beyond a favorable outcome.

column5: food blessings traced to manna and land
column6: The commentary places praise after a received benefit; the rabbis attribute the blessings after meals to Moses at the manna, Joshua on entering the land, and David and Solomon at Jerusalem, reading Israel's liturgy through successive gifts.

column5: command to declare God's deeds to the living
column6: The commentary says the recipient should tell others about the giver's favor; Raphael tells Tobit and Tobias to bless God, give thanks, and declare God's works before all the living.

column5: a victory hymn directed to God
column6: The commentary says a beneficiary answers good with public praise; after Israel's deliverance Judith begins a song to her God with instruments.

column5: singing a new song for God's strength
column6: The commentary describes praise that tells the giver's deeds; Judith sings a new song to God and praises his greatness and invincible power.

column5: the delivered people bless God's holy name
column6: The commentary makes praise follow received deliverance; Wisdom says the righteous sang praise and blessed God's holy name after their rescue.
The commentary says God's favor includes the capacity to praise; Wisdom says the divine Wisdom opened the mouths of the mute and made the tongues of infants clear.

column5: food given so people may thank the creator
column6: The commentary says recipients answer God's provision with hamd; the post-meal prayer says God gave food and drink to humanity so that people might thank him, then names the community's spiritual food and drink.
